COMMUNITY HELPERS WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Sanitation Worker — solve it right on the sheet.

Trace SANITATION WORKER, match the worker to the garbage truck, the recycling bin and the safety gloves, circle the items that can be recycled, count the recycling bins and draw one way to keep your neighborhood clean.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then trace, match, circle, count and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

← PhotographerPrevious activitySchool Counselor →Next activity
HOW TO DO IT

Five little steps.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted words SANITATION WORKER — two long words for the people who keep the town clean.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the sanitation worker to the garbage truck, the recycling bin and the safety gloves.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Six items sit in the grid — circle every one that can be recycled. Four really can; the last two go somewhere else — one to the compost, one to the trash!

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the recycling bins, then write the number in the box.

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw one way to keep your neighborhood clean in the big box — bins in a row, a litter pickup, or your family sorting the recycling.

Ask a grown-up to read the steps aloud the first time. After that, you know just what to do.

YOUR PENCIL CASE

Pick your tools.

Pencil, nine crayons, an eraser, undo, redo and clear — the tools appear right here and work on the sheet. Save keeps your finished work as a picture, and your saved work comes back next time.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What sanitation workers do for the whole town, which items go in the recycling bin, and where the rest belongs — compost, trash or the bin — plus how to write the words SANITATION WORKER.

Knowledge to have ready: Sanitation workers keep the town clean and healthy: the garbage truck empties the trash, the recycling bin waits for bottles, cans, jars and cardboard, and the safety gloves protect strong hands. Here is the sorting secret — a banana peel is not trash to a garden: it composts into food for new plants!

Why this activity matters: This sheet explains the people behind the early-morning rumble — helpers children hear every week but rarely meet. The recycle-or-not grid builds real sorting skills your own kitchen bin can use tonight, and the safety rule is worth its weight: never chase or hide near a working truck.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Recycling awareness
  • Sorting practice
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Neighborhood drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a sanitation worker — the helper who keeps our whole town clean and healthy. Trace the two words, then connect the garbage truck, the recycling bin and the gloves. Now the six items: which ones can be recycled? One is a snack’s coat and one is a snack itself! Count the bins, and then draw how WE keep our streets clean."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the gloves and ask what they protect the hands from. In the grid, sort out loud: bottle, box, can, jar — yes to the recycling bin; the crinkly bag and the peel take other roads. The peel is the happy one: it becomes compost, food for the garden. In the count row, count the bins curb to curb.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the garbage truck do on our street?" "Which four things go in the recycling bin?" "Where does the banana peel go instead — and what does it become?" "What do the safety gloves do?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: Two items in the grid are not for the recycling bin — one is shiny and crinkly, and one used to be fruit. Ask of each: recycle bin, compost pile, or trash can? The garden would love one of them.

Parent tips: Trucks and bins are work zones: keep little watchers well back on collection day — never behind a reversing truck, never inside a bin. Then sort tonight’s recycling together and let your child be the checker: bottle, box, can, jar — the sheet, done for real.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who keeps our town clean? Name two things that can be recycled. Where does the banana peel go?" The worker, two recyclables, the compost = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Start a small compost jar or corner this week for peels and apple cores — let your child feed it daily and watch it change. The grid’s trickiest tile becomes a living science experiment on the windowsill.

This activity belongs to Class 33 — Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood on the Learning Path. Progress is saved on this device for the child chosen in My Classroom — and only a real save of finished work marks it cleared, never just opening the page.
